title: Comparing and choosing
job: More, less, better — stating a preference
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: A + è + più + Adj + di + B
A + è + più + Adj + che + Adj
A + è + migliore / peggiore + di + B

rules.text: ITALIAN FORCES A CHOICE ENGLISH DOES NOT HAVE. più … DI compares two things on one quality: Roma è più grande di Milano. più … CHE compares two qualities, two verbs or two phrases about the SAME thing: È più bello che utile. The working rule is short — di before a noun or a pronoun, che before anything else — and English's single "than" gives no signal at all.

The comparative costs this module no new function words. che is already L1-M5's and di is L1-M1's, so both rows simply take on a second job. The work here is the CHOICE between them, not the vocabulary — which is worth saying, because a learner who is hunting for a word to learn will miss the whole lesson.

migliore against meglio is Italian keeping apart what English merges. migliore is the ADJECTIVE — È il ristorante migliore — and meglio is the ADVERB — Si mangia meglio qui. English says "better" for both and Spanish uses mejor for both, so this delta runs the opposite way from every other comparison in the level. peggiore and peggio do the same.

preferire brings the -isc- verbs, a third of the third conjugation: preferisco, preferisci, preferisce — with the infix in the singular and the third plural and absent from noi and voi. capire and finire do the same. It is a shape rather than an irregularity, and once seen it covers dozens of verbs.

quello apocopates in front of a noun exactly as M3's bello does, and tracks the same articles: quel libro, quell'uomo, quei libri. questo does not shorten at all. That pairing — one demonstrative that bends and one that does not — is the cheapest way to hold both.

sentences.display: Roma è più grande di Milano
sentences.literal: Rome is more big of Milan

words.note: The comparative marker, and it goes in front of the adjective — Italian never changes the adjective's ending for a comparison. M7's più tardi kept this word waiting for exactly this row.
più's opposite, built the same way: meno grande. It also does the quarter-to on a clock — le sette meno un quarto — which M6 pointed forward to.

sentences.trap: The comparison is di because Milano is a noun. Swap in an adjective and it becomes che — and that one decision is the whole grammar of this module.
sentences.sound: pyoo GRAN-de dee mee-LA-no. più is one syllable, and the accent marks its stress.

variations.changed: the other way round, and M3's adjective agreeing

variations.display: Roma è meno cara di Milano
variations.cue: Rome is less expensive than Milan

variations.display: Il treno è più caro del biglietto
variations.cue: The train is more expensive than the ticket

mistake.display: Roma è più grande che Milano
mistake.why: Before a noun it is di: Roma è più grande di Milano.

sentences.usage: Comparing two places, two prices, two anything.
sentences.mnemonic: di before a noun. che before everything else.

words.note: An -e adjective, so two cells. The u is fully sounded — OO-tee-le — and the stress is on the first syllable.

sentences.trap: Two adjectives about ONE thing, so che. Nothing is being compared with anything else here — the sentence weighs two qualities of the same object, and that is what che is for.
sentences.sound: e pyoo BEL-lo ke OO-tee-le. che is one short syllable with a hard k.

mistake.why: Two qualities take che: È più bello che utile.

sentences.usage: The verdict with a reservation in it — and it is a very Italian shape.

words.note: The adjective. It describes a noun — il ristorante migliore — and it can never describe a verb, which is meglio's job.
The adverb, invariable. Si mangia meglio qui — one eats better here. English uses "better" for both and gives no warning at all.
An -e noun, so its plural is in -i. A trattoria is smaller and plainer, and the words are not interchangeable.

sentences.trap: migliore describes a thing and meglio describes an action. Getting them the wrong way round is the single commonest Italian mistake an English or Spanish speaker makes.
sentences.sound: mee-LYO-re. The gli is the soft ly of figlio and famiglia.

variations.cue: The food is worse in Rome

mistake.why: A noun takes the adjective: È il ristorante migliore.

sentences.usage: Recommending somewhere, and it is the sentence that gets asked for most.
sentences.mnemonic: migliore describes a thing, meglio an action.

words.note: migliore's opposite, and an adjective in the same way. Il peggiore is the worst one.
meglio's opposite, invariable, and only ever about an action. The pair maps onto migliore and meglio exactly.

sentences.trap: M4's impersonal si is back, and it is what makes this sentence about eating in general rather than about anyone. Si mangia is "one eats" — the food, judged by how it is eaten.
sentences.sound: see MAN-ja PEJ-jo kwee. Both g's of peggio are one long soft j.

variations.changed: the adjective, about the place itself

variations.display: Qui si mangia meglio che a Roma
variations.cue: The food is better here than in Rome
variations.changed: with a comparison — and che, because a phrase follows

mistake.why: An action takes the adverb: Si mangia peggio qui.

sentences.usage: Comparing two places to eat, which is a national pastime.

words.note: For choosing among things in view. It is a sibling of L1-M5's che cosa, not a form of it — che cosa asks what a thing is, quale asks which one.

sentences.trap: The superlative is the same più with an article in front of the noun. Italian has no separate "most" ending — il libro più bello does the whole job, and only the article marks it as a superlative.
sentences.sound: e eel LEE-bro pyoo BEL-lo. The article is what carries the superlative meaning.

mistake.why: The superlative needs its article: È il libro più bello.

sentences.usage: Picking the best of several, in a shop or off a list.
sentences.mnemonic: The article makes it the most.

words.note: An -isc- verb: the infix appears in io, tu, lui and loro and vanishes in noi and voi. capire and finire behave the same way, so this is a class rather than an oddity.
For what is here. It never shortens, unlike quello — which is the easiest way to keep the two apart.

sentences.trap: questo stands alone here with no noun after it. It is a pronoun as well as an adjective, and Italian needs no "one" the way English does.
sentences.sound: pre-fe-REES-ko KWE-sto. The isc is where the stress lands.

variations.changed: the tu cell, with the same infix

mistake.why: This class takes the infix: Preferisco questo.

sentences.usage: In a shop, choosing between two things on the counter.
sentences.mnemonic: -isc- in the singular, gone in noi and voi.

words.note: For what is over there. Standing alone it keeps its full shape — Preferisco quello — and only shortens when a noun follows.
The shortened form, tracking the article the noun would take — exactly as M3's bel does. quel libro, because it is il libro.
The third-person cell, still with the infix. Cosa preferisce? is what a waiter asks.

sentences.trap: quello shortens and questo does not, and that is the only difference in how they behave. Learning them as a pair is cheaper than learning quello's four shapes alone.
sentences.sound: kwel LEE-bro. quel is one syllable and runs straight into the noun.

feminine — and it does not shorten
the polite question a waiter asks

mistake.why: In front of an il-word it shortens: Preferisco quel libro.

sentences.usage: Pointing at something across a counter or a room.
sentences.mnemonic: questo never shortens. quello always might.

words.note: The plural of quel, for nouns that take i — quei libri. It is bei's exact counterpart, and the article is again what chooses it.
The elided shape, which fuses with its noun into ONE index key. quell'uomo is a single word to the engine, exactly as M3's bell'uomo is.

sentences.trap: Four shapes again, tracking four articles — il, l', i, gli. Once the articles are known, quello and bello cost nothing extra: they are the same rule twice.
sentences.sound: kway LEE-bree. quei is one syllable with a gliding vowel.

variations.changed: a vowel, so the elided form
feminine plural, which does not shorten

mistake.why: In front of an i-word it is quei: Quei libri sono più cari.

sentences.usage: Comparing things at a distance — a shelf, a menu, a display.
sentences.mnemonic: quello and bello are one rule twice.

sentences.display: Questo è più caro di quello
sentences.cue: This one is more expensive than that one
sentences.literal: This is more dear of that

words.note: The feminine of questo, standing alone. Questa è più cara — no noun needed, because the ending says which thing is meant.
The plurals, and neither shortens. questi libri, queste case — the article is not involved at all.

sentences.trap: quello is a pronoun here, so it keeps its full shape. It only ever shortens in front of a noun, and there is no noun after it in this sentence.
sentences.sound: KWE-sto e pyoo KA-ro dee KWEL-lo. The two demonstratives frame the line.

words.note: The tu cell, and the last of the infix set this module shows. Cosa preferisci? is what a friend asks over a menu.

sentences.trap: che rather than di, because what follows is a phrase and not a noun. a Roma is a preposition plus a place, and the rule catches it exactly.
sentences.sound: kwee see MAN-ja ME-lyo ke a RO-ma. meglio has the soft ly in the middle.
